did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 73 opens with the heading “A psalm of Asaph” and a foundational declaration: God is good to Israel and to those whose hearts are pure. From the very beginning, the psalm presents the tension between the poet’s faith and what he sees in reality.

Did you know? The poet honestly admits that he became envious when he saw the prosperity of the wicked. The psalm does not hide the question of faith; instead, it describes how the apparent success of the wicked unsettles the righteous.

Did you know? The wicked are described as appearing healthy, peaceful, and free from the troubles that afflict other people. This description emphasizes that the problem is not merely their wealth, but the gap between their apparent success and the expectation of divine justice.

Did you know? The speech of the wicked is portrayed as a central part of their arrogance: they speak with oppression, exalt themselves with their words, and even question God’s knowledge and providence.

Did you know? At the heart of his crisis, the poet asks whether he has kept his heart pure and washed his hands in innocence for nothing. In other words, he wonders whether moral integrity and faithfulness to God have any meaning when the righteous themselves suffer.

Did you know? The turning point in the psalm occurs when the poet enters God’s sanctuary. There he understands the destiny of the wicked, after previously struggling to make sense of reality based only on outward appearances.

Did you know? After understanding their fate, the poet compares the success of the wicked to a dream: it seems real while one is asleep, but disappears upon waking. The image emphasizes the temporary nature of their prosperity.

Did you know? The poet does not blame only the wicked; he also examines himself and recognizes that his bitterness and confusion resulted from a lack of understanding. He describes himself as “brutish” and like an animal before God, meaning that he failed to grasp the whole picture.

Did you know? Despite the crisis, the poet discovers that God has not abandoned him: “Yet I am always with you.” God is described as holding his right hand, guiding him with counsel, and leading him to glory.

Did you know? The psalm’s conclusion is that “nearness to God” is the poet’s true good. He chooses to make God his refuge and to proclaim all his works, having understood that closeness to God matters more than outward prosperity.
